14. Conclusions and research priorities
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing is not optical metal fusion. It is patterned formation of a metal-filled photopolymer green
body followed by binder removal and metallurgical densification. Its potential for fine geometry and smooth surfaces comes from a
coupled powder–binder–light–layer system whose optical and rheological demands compete. The green object must then be recovered and
cleaned without damage, converted to a porous brown body without internal pressure or residue, and sintered under controlled gravity,
setter and atmosphere conditions.
  A defensible industrial programme follows five rules:
 1. qualify powder, photoreactive binder, additives, mixture and delivery architecture as one time-dependent feedstock system;
 2. measure spectrum, irradiance field, scattering, cure depth, lateral growth and green state instead of transferring wavelength, dose or
    pixel pitch;
 3. keep exposed, cleaned green, brown, sintered, HIPed, heat-treated, machined and delivered states separate;
 4. qualify cleaning access, debinding, shrinkage, setters and final properties on representative geometry and furnace loads; and
 5. compare LMM with other routes using accepted complete-cell throughput, safety, yield and part-linked evidence.
    Priority research should improve in-line dispersion and sedimentation metrology; rheology-to-layer-transfer models for suspension and
paste architectures; three-dimensional light transport in metal-filled media; spatially resolved conversion metrology for highly loaded and
opaque green bodies; validated conversion surrogates with uncertainty and debinding correlation; oxygen/stabiliser and degassing/re-
aeration maps at permeable interfaces; conversion and particle-packing maps; optical-field calibration tied to final geometry; non-
destructive detection of trapped feedstock and green cracks; geometry-aware cleaning and debinding transport; brown-state monitoring;
shrinkage/setter/friction models; small-feature inspection with quantified probability of detection; material-specific chemistry control for
copper, NiTi, tungsten and other advanced metals; and transfer protocols across feedstock batches, machines and furnaces.
    Until those links close for a specified route, claims such as “pixel resolution,” “support-free,” “any metal,” “powder-free,” “safe,”
“zero waste,” “MIM-equivalent,” “fully dense,” “high throughput” and one shrinkage factor remain incomplete. The capability belongs to
a qualified powder–photoactive-binder–layer-delivery–optical–cleaning–thermal–post-process–factory system.

J Segurola. Lithography-based metal manufacturing: metal-filled photoresins, cure–loading trade-offs, debinding, sintering and qualification. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt identifies several debinding challenges specific to crosslinked acrylate photopolymers in metal vat photopolymerization. The starting green body is spatially non-uniform: crosslink density, optical conversion history, powder/binder distribution, section thickness, cleaning residues, and feature accessibility determine how decomposition gases and solvents travel. Overexposure can increase crosslinking and reduce accessibility, while undercure and conversion gradients can produce weak or unevenly decomposing regions. Binder shrinkage constrained around rigid metal particles may generate interfacial stress, microcracks, weakened particle bridges, and non-uniform transport paths, increasing gas-pressure damage during thermal debinding. Qualification therefore requires geometry- and load-specific testing rather than relying only on nominal binder percentage; thermogravimetric or evolved-gas analysis can screen actual feedstock but does not establish full-part suitability. Water-, solvent-, catalytic-, and direct-thermal routes are not interchangeable and depend on the cured network, powder surface, cleaning history, feature openness, and furnace state. The excerpt does not provide a direct comparison with conventional MIM binders, a maximum wall-thickness limit, or numerical residual carbon/oxygen limits for sintered steel, copper, or titanium. It only notes that chemistry must be verified and that evidence such as mass/gas response, chemistry, and integrity is needed.

           Recent Advances in the Biomedical Field with the Lithography-based Metal
                                 Manufacturing Process

      Gyoergy HARAKALY1*, Santiago CANO CANO1, Johannes BOSTERS1, Clemens SPERLING1, Denise
                      MOEDDER1 and Gerald MITTERAMSKOGLER1

                                     1Incus GmbH, Christine-Touaillon-Str. 11, Vienna, 1220, Austria.

       Abstract
        Lithography-Based Metal Manufacturing (LMM) emerges as an advanced additive manufacturing (AM) technology dedicated
         to crafting functional metal components with superior surface aesthetics and heightened  feature resolutions compared to
         alternative AM methodologies. LMM employs the concept of photopolymerization  in metal manufacturing, where metal
       powder is intricately dispersed within a light-sensitive resin, forming a three-dimensional structure through layered exposure
         to light.
       The printed components undergo a subsequent debinding and sintering process, akin to other sinter-based metal manufacturing
         technologies. Following these steps, mechanical properties comparable to those achieved through Metal Injection Molding
      (MIM) can be realized. Additionally, the as-sintered parts exhibit Ra surface roughness values below 2 μm.
        In this work, we explore recent advances in the biomedical field, showcasing application examples in dentistry and surgical
          tools. Alloys of steels and titanium find utility in these applications, exemplifying the versatility of LMM in contributing  to
        advancements within the healthcare sector.

       Keywords: Stereolithography, Biomedical Industry, Sinter-based additive manufacturing

        Introduction
        Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized various application fields, with the biomedical field being one of its most
        transformative areas. This technology allows, due to its (typically) layer-wise production approach, the creation of complex
        geometries,  which are  often  commercially  not  suitable  for manufacturing  or downright impossible with  traditional
         technologies.
    AM is an established technology and wide research effort undertaken to exploit it in various fields of the medical industry, be
             it pharmaceutical drug production1), printing of polymer or ceramic parts2) or tissue printing with the various bioprinting
         techniques3). Metal printing technologies are mostly used for the development and production of various implants currently.
       Powder Bed Fusion (PBF) techniques are most commonly utilized for this purpose,4) namely Selective Laser Sintering,
         Selective Laser Melting and Electron Beam Melting. Thus, the material selection mostly follows the technical potential of
        these techniques5) with research on other materials, as well as on other technologies are actively performed.
      As most of the current part selection of AM produced medical parts comes from the PBF process, issues of poor surface
          characteristics, poor dimensional accuracy and control of the microstructure needs research attention for this specific processes.
        Furthermore, there  is a myriad of variations of medical  devices, implants and geometries, which must requires strong
         standardization effort.6)
       However, the advantages of AM, the high level of customization potential, good precision, a rapid design to product speed,
         the potential for improved functional performance, and the cost effectiveness in small to mid batch-size production are
        supporting the AM-biomedical  field and  its push towards personalized medicine  solutions. As already described, many
         different applications in the biomedical field are already utilizing various AM methodologies. Here we are focusing on the
         current market  for metal  materials, and the potential  solutions  for these applications  with Lithography-based Metal
        Manufacturing (LMM) process.

    LMM process
       The LMM technology, developed by Incus GmbH, is an additive manufacturing process based on stereolithography principles.
        This method leverages digital light processing (DLP) to fabricate metal parts. The process begins with a photoreactive binder
        formulation  in which  metal powder  is  dispersed. Upon UV  irradiation,  this  mixture  undergoes  a  layer-by-layer
        photopolymerization,  creating a three-dimensional  structure. The resulting polymer matrix encapsulates the metal powders,
        forming stable green parts with sufficient mechanical strength for further processing.
      As printing material, a mixture of powder and organic binder, referred as feedstock, is designed to be solid at room temperature
        with a sharp transition from solid to liquid at elevated temperatures between 35 and 60 °C. The material is introduced into the
         printer in block form, and a heated wiper blade spreads a thin, uniform film onto the build area. UV irradiation selectively
        cures the film, and after each layer is cured, the build platform descends to allow the application of a new layer of material
         (Fig. 1). Between the coating steps, the material is cooled below room temperature to allow quick solidification. This material
        has enough strength to sufficiently support the polymerized layers, eliminating the need of additional support structures during

         the process.





                                                       Fig. 1. The LMM printing process

       The printers utilizing the LMM technology feature high-performance projection units that facilitate the shaping process. A
       top-down approach of irradiation is employed to polymerize the feedstock. This allows the utilization of the unique feedstock,
       which prevents powder sedimentation, and ensures that no excess stress is exerted on the parts during fabrication, enhancing
          their structural integrity.
       Once the shaping process completed, the uncured material can be removed through a simple melting process, called decaking
         (Fig. 2). The decaking involves heating the system to 40-80 °C under air to melt the uncured feedstock and release the green
          parts, facilitating  easy recovery and operational  safety. The excess material can be reintroduced to the LMM-printer for
        subsequent printing. This material recyclability process ensures a resource-efficient and environmentally friendly production
        methodology.
        Following a fine cleaning with a solvent, the green parts undergo debinding and sintering, similar to Metal Injection Molding
        process, to achieve their final metallic form. This process firstly removes the organic matter to form a porous brown part,
       which is then densified through sintering to achieve the final metallic component.





                             Fig. 2. The decaking process at different moment (left: early stage; right: later stage)

       For the LMM process, MIM-grade, gas-atomized spherical metal powders are typically used, although other types, such as
        water-atomized powders, can also be employed. For the parts presented in this study, metal powders with a size distribution
        of 0-25 micrometers are standardly used. The sintering conditions for the various metal materials discussed in this study largely
       depend on the material, the powder supplier, and are often proprietary information specific to the end users of the technology.

## 2. harakaly2025recentadvancesin pages 2-5 (Context ID: pqac-00000020)

Metal AM has mostly impacted the surgical field with the creation of surgical instrument solutions, which can improve the
         precision and efficacy of complex procedures. The opportunity to develop novel tools to enhance the doctor performance by
        improving control and precision can improve overall surgical outcomes. Furthermore, by utilizing the unique flexibility of AM
         for individualization, patient specific parts also can be manufactured, which supports the push towards personalized healthcare.
       For every surgical procedure, the precision of the part geometry is paramount. LMM uses the stereolithography principle,
       which intrinsically provides high precision, as the resolution of the sintered parts is expected to be below the half of the pixel
         size of the used DLP projector unit for printing. For example, in the Hammer Lab 35 printer a 35 µm feature resolution
         projector is utilized, which brings the sintered tolerance to a maximum of ±17 µm, before post-machining procedures. This
        brings this technology an optimal method for production of especially small geometries.
        Small and precise parts are desired in some exact surgery procedures, where high precision can decide the well-being of the




                                                     “Journal of the Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy” Vol. 72 Supplement                                                                                                           S1229


          patients. Such processes are endoscopic surgeries, neurosurgeries and cardiovascular surgeries. As case study part, a miniature
         gripper tool can be seen in Fig. 3. This tool offers precise manipulation within the confined spaces, and provides high level of
         control and maneuverability during laparoscopic interventions. The design of the gripper and the smooth as-sintered surface
        (below 2 µm arithmetic average surface roughness) of the LMM produced part minimizes tissue trauma and enable accurate
         tissue handling, making it a vital instrument for minimally invasive procedures. Due to the size of the geometry, the production
        of this component with both traditional and other additive manufacturing technologies  is difficult, making the use of LMM
        technology more economically feasible compared to those methodologies.





                                             Fig. 3. 316L stainless steel laparoscopic microgripper

       During orthodontic surgeries, precision of the geometry is paramount as well, as non-optimal parts could cause complications,
         in worst case scenario even nerve damage. Thus, customized implant guides and drills, which fit the dental structure of the
         individual patients, have high potential as application for LMM processes. The orthodontics industry using wide variety of
        metal materials for its purposes, for example various stainless steel alloys, Cobalt Chrome and alloys of Titanium are well
         established in various applications.7) The precision of LMM allows printing of threaded screws which are fully functional,
       making it a potential methodology for the production of dental screws as well (Fig. 4.).





                                             Fig. 4. LMM printed dental screw from Ti6Al4V alloy

       However, a much more relevant application, especially for AM is the field of dental reconstruction. AM is already well utilized
         in this field, especially ceramic printing methodologies.8) For example, dental brackets, tailored to the patients dental anatomy,
        can improve the effectiveness of the treatment. LMM printed parts have low surface roughness, with numbers below 2 µm of
         arithmetic average surface roughness (Ra),9) which make subsequent polishing operations economically more feasible. This is
         significant in the field of metal brackets production, as high level of polish is desired by the patients of the application  (Fig.
          5). Furthermore, surface roughness characteristic affects the corrosion properties of AM parts, which also makes the polishing
         potential and economics an important factor.10)

        Metal AM also have entered in the field of orthopedic or bone replacement implants, such as hip and knee replacements, or
         cranial and maxillofacial implants. Currently mostly Powder Bed Fusion technologies are utilized for this purpose. The most
        used materials are various Titanium alloys, which elucidate the used technology, as currently difficult to reach medical standard
        approved properties  with sinter-based  technologies. However, Powder Bed Fusion technologies  need extensive  post-
        processing to reach the desired part qualities, making the potential designs limited. Incus is actively undertaking development
         efforts to reach the necessary chemical composition for medical grade Ti6Al4V alloy (grade 5). Currently the carbon values
        of the sintered parts are higher than requested (around 0.11 wt.% compared to the 0.08 wt.%, described in the standards).
       However, mechanical values are already achieving good values, such as 900 MPa yield strength and 960 MPa ultimate tensile
         strength.
      CoCr is also commonly used implant material, especially at load-bearing implants.11) It is also a common material in sinter-
        based technologies, thus parts are able to be produced with LMM too. It is also an interesting material for other applications,
         as example for audiology implants (Fig. 6.).





                        Fig. 6. LMM printed audiology implant design (design and photo courtesy of Metshape GmbH)

      To ensure better osteointegration of bone replacement materials,  structuring the surface of the implant. Furthermore, by
        designing the surface according to the forces, which the part become under during its lifetime, the friction-induced wear can
       be also reduced. LMM can be used to fabricate exact surfaces. Melentiev et al.12) have proved that by printing an artificial
          articular hip prosthesis with 150 µm wide and 50 µm deep microdimples.





                                        Fig. 6. Artificial articular prosthesis and its surface patterning12)

       Conclusion

       The advantages of AM, including the customization potential and improved functional performance, is significantly benefiting
         the biomedical field and have strong potential to support the direction towards personalized medicine. LMM technology, with
            its high precision and efficiency, is particularly suitable for producing intricate components, which can be essential for surgical
       and dental applications. Creation of precise instruments enhance the success rate and safety of complex procedures.
       Although challenges  are present for certain applications, such as further development necessary to reach medical grade
       Ti6Al4V alloy, LMM shows strong potential to be a technology which offers new possibilities for surgical instruments, dental
         applications, and in the future, orthopedic and bone replacement implants.

                                                                         2                                                                                  Abstract

   English Abstract
NASA Glenn Research Copper GRCop-42 (Cu-4 at.% Cr-2 at.% Nb) is recognised for its
remarkable strength, creep resistance, and conductivity. It was designed for application in
fusion-based additive manufacturing methods, including powder bed fusion and selective laser
melting. Chromium and Niobium enhance the  material's strength through  precipitation
hardening via the intermetallic phase Cr2Nb. Although Cr2Nb significantly enhances the
properties of GRCop-42, it also impedes pressureless sintering. Consequently, limited research
has been conducted on sinter-based additive manufacturing utilising GRCop-42, as pressureless
solid-state sintering of GRCop-42 is impractical. This study aims to examine whether the
incorporation of additional alloys or elements can facilitate pressureless liquid phase sintering
in GRCop-42 by enhancing wettability. Copper-Tin 90/10 Bronze and Silver were selected.
These should supply adequate liquid phase and capillary force for densification. The disruption
of the stable oxide layer and mass transport via the liquid phase could be accomplished for both
Bronze 90/10 and Silver. In both instances, Cr2Nb underwent dissociation via oxidation owing
to the elevated Oxygen affinity of Niobium. This was induced by trace amounts of water in the
hydrogen sinter atmosphere due to its elevated chemical reactivity. This led to a deterioration
of the wettability of the liquid phase.

Die von der NASA Glenn Research entwickelte ternäre Kupferlegierung GRCop-42 (Cu-4 at

entwickelt, darunter Pulverbettschmelzen und selektives Laserschmelzen. Chrom und Niob

untersuchen, ob die Verwendung zusätzlicher Legierungen oder Elemente das drucklose

diesem Zweck wurden Kupfer-Zinn Bronze 90/10 und Silber ausgewählt. Diese sollten eine
ausreichende Flüssigphase und Kapillarkraft für die Verdichtung liefern. Die Durchbrechung
der stabilen Oxidschicht und der Stofftransport über die Flüssigphase konnten sowohl bei der

erhöhten Sauerstoffaffinität von Niob einer Dissoziation durch Oxidation. Dies wurde durch
Spuren von Wasser in der Wasserstoff-Sinteratmosphäre aufgrund ihrer erhöhten chemischen
Reaktivität  ausgelöst.  Dies  führte  zu  einer  Verschlechterung  der  Benetzbarkeit  der
Flüssigphase.





                                                                           4                                                                Introduction and Motivation

1.Introduction and Motivation
   1.1. Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionised a wide range of application technologies,
ranging from ceramics, metallurgy, plastics technologies, all the way to biomedical. The many
different AM methods used today are employed in fields such as manufacturing, defence,
aviation, automotive, healthcare, pharmaceutical industries and many more.[1, 2] Depending
on the application needed, all these sectors can draw upon a plethora of different metal additive
manufacturing (MAM) methods such as binder jetting (BJ), powder bed fusion (PBF), material
extrusion (ME), selective laser sintering (SLS), direct energy deposition (DED) as well as many
more.[3] One of the emerging methods employed in MAM  is Lithography-based Metal
Manufacturing (LMM). It is an attractive alternative which enables the fabrication of small
parts with high resolutions. LMM takes advantage of stereolithography (SLA) and Digital Light
Processing (DLP)  in combination with powder metallurgy.[4] Powder metallurgy  is a
manufacturing technique with a long history dating back to the 1920s.[5] While many MAM
methods frequently produce parts with poor surface and dimensional characteristics, in addition
to limited control over the microstructure, LMM can chiefly eliminate these restrictions. It also
enables the production of parts that require minimal post-treatment.[6] While alloys such as
316L steel have been successfully used for LMM at TU Wien, metals such as Copper and its
alloys are not yet fully developed. Copper is especially useful because it offers a wide range of
applications due to  its high thermal and electrical conductivity.  It is also classified as a
“Strategic Raw Material” by the European Union, which increases the value of manufacturing
techniques such as LMM, which make efficient use of materials.[7] While Copper offers great
conductivity, it lacks mechanical strength. This makes it difficult to use pure copper in high-
tech fields such as aerospace and energy.[8] A remedy to this problem is ternary Copper alloys,
which combine the good properties of Copper with increased mechanical properties such as
creep resistance, low cycle fatigue, as well as strength. This is commonly achieved through
particle-based dispersion strengthening.[9] Although many ternary Copper systems exist, the
most promising in terms of its mechanical capabilities is the Copper-Chromium-Niobium (Cu-
Cr-Nb) system. While a plethora of Cu-Cr-Nb systems with varying amounts of alloying metals
exist, a very common alloy in the field of aerospace is NASA Glenn Research Copper (GRCop),
GRCop-42 (Cu-4 at.% Cr-2 at.% Nb).[8–11] Currently, commonly employed AM techniques
for GRCop-42 are laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) or electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-
PBF), Graded Alloy Processing, and laser powder direct energy deposition (LP-DED).[11–13]
These AM methods all have in common that they do not share the process of sintering found in
classic powder metallurgy as well as LMM processes. No literature could be found which tried
to combine GRCop-42 with LMM and, therefore, atmospheric sintering. The first aim of this
work was to examine whether GRCop-42 could be printed using existing LMM technologies
based on copper LMM applications. The second target was to examine whether GRCop-42
could be sintered using traditional atmospheric sintering methods. This would be needed to
make the combination of GRCop-42 and LMM possible.

                                                                        5                                                                    Theoretical Background

2.Theoretical Background
   2.1. LMM
Since its commercial emergence in the second half of the 1980s, additive manufacturing has
made monumental strides in development and production.[14, 15] Since its inception, it has
enabled designers to shift the focus from productibility towards optimal functionality. This has
made AM a vital part of sectors like aerospace, both civilian and military, ranging from aircraft
to  satellites.  Today AM  has  also  reached  sectors  such  as  chemical  engineering,
microelectronics, civil engineering and many more, thanks to its rapid development.[16] In
comparison to other AM methods employed in the sector of metallurgy, such as PBF, SLS,
SLM and Electron Beam Melting (EBM), which often exhibit poor surface characteristics, poor
dimensional accuracy and limited control over the microstructure, Lithography-based additive
manufacturing (LAM) and its derivative LMM have garnered attention as a potential remedy
to these problems.[6] All LAM methods have in common that a photosensitive liquid or

   2.2. Liquid phase sintering
With the green part obtained, the next step is sintering. The driving force for sintering is the
reduction of the Gibbs energy ΔG between the initial state and final state of the system. This is
accomplished through the reduction of external (boundary surfaces, walls of pores accessible
from the outside) and internal (walls of enclosed pores, grain boundaries) surfaces. In general,
closely packed particles sinter when being heated near their melting point. As particle size
decreases and the temperature approaches the melting point, sintering speeds up. While smaller
particles result in a larger surface area (bigger difference), heat provides the necessary
activation energy to reduce the Gibbs energy, through the elimination of pores, their rounding
and the coarsening of pores and particles.[22] Sintering is the main method for producing dense,
near-net shape work pieces in powder metallurgy (PM).[23] Two main types of sintering exist:
solid phase sintering and liquid phase sintering (LPS). In LPS, a liquid phase coexists with solid
particles, at high temperature, over a period of time during the sintering process.[22, 24] At the
bare minimum, two chemical elements are required. One element serves as the one which stays
solid, this is the major component and another or several minor components which melt and
promote LPS. These minor components can either melt on their own or form a lower melting
eutectic with the main component.[24] Usually, the solid grains are also soluble (at least to
some extent) in the forming liquid phase.[22] The metal powders used can either be a mixture
of several metal powders or be a pre-alloyed powder, which allows for homogeneous
distribution of the alloying elements throughout the powder.[24] A wide variety of factors
related to the metal powder have an effect on LPS. The size, shape, and distribution of grains
and porosity, along with grain contiguity and connectivity, also play a role in LPS. At the start

Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a relatively recent manufacturing method which
has become a key area of interest in multiple industrial sectors. Deriving from
digital models (CAD data or 3D scans), the process can be used to create solid yet
highly complex parts by joining materials, usually layer upon layer as opposed
to subtractive manufacturing methods. Additive manufacturing is also called 3D
printing, additive fabrication or freeform fabrication. Features of AM like freedom
of part design, part complexity, light weighting, part consolidation and design
for function are garnering particular interests in metal additive manufacturing
for aerospace, oil and gas, marine and automobile applications and are pushing
towards a tool-less manufacturing environment.
There are many AM techniques available which can be roughly categorized
according to their raw material. They are (1) powder-based, (2) liquid-based, and
(3) solid-based. Some examples of powder-based techniques include selective laser
melting (SLM), selective laser sintering (SLS), and electron beam melting (EBM).
Liquid-based techniques include vat-polymerization (VP)/stereolithography
apparatus (SLA), digital light processing (DLP) and polyjet or binder jetting (BJ).
Solid-based techniques include laminated object manufacturing (LOM) and fused
filament fabrication (FFF)/material extrusion (ME), formerly known as fused
deposition modelling (FDM). [As a side note, fused deposition modelling (FDM)
is now a brand name of Stratasys and can no longer be used as a descriptive term
for the process itself.] Basically, any material can be produced by one or another
AM technique today.
In jewelry making, 3D-printed molds of the models, typically made from wax or
resin, quickly found a widespread application, replacing the tool-based or hand-
formed wax models used in investment casting. There are also tailored SLM
machines on the market for jewelry applications,1 allowing to 3D-print whole
pieces from stainless steel, titanium or precious metal alloys. However, due to

    Sinter-Based Additive Metal Manufacturing
     The novel lithography-based metal manufacturing (LMM) technology  is an
     evolution of the processes of vat-polymerization (VP) and the technology of metal
      injection molding (MIM).


    Metal Injection Molding (MIM)
   MIM gained recognition throughout the 1990s as improving cost efficiency
      of complex-shaped metal parts through high-volume production to net-shape,
     negating costly, additional operations such as machining. The MIM process steps,
     as illustrated in Figure 1,9 involve combining metal powders with polymers such
     as wax and thermoplastic binders to produce the feedstock mix that is injected as a
      liquid into a mold using plastic injection molding machines. The molded or green
      part is cooled and ejected from the mold. Next, a portion of the binder material is
    removed using solvent, thermal furnaces, catalytic process, or a combination of
     methods. The resulting fragile and porous part is in a condition called the brown
       stage.

Sintering heats the powder to temperatures near the melting point in a protective
atmosphere furnace to densify the particles using capillary forces in a process
called sintering. Due to the small particle size of the powders, diffusion rates
are high, leading to reproducible shrinkage between approximately 15 and 25%
(depending on the feedstock system employed) and densification in the range
of 96–99% solid density. The end-product metal has comparable mechanical
and physical properties with annealed parts made using classic metalworking
methods. Post-sintering heat treatments for MIM are the same as with other
fabrication routes, and with high density the MIM component is compatible
with the metal conditioning treatments such as plating, passivating, annealing,
carburizing, nitriding, and precipitation hardening.
The window of economic advantage in metal injection molded parts lies in
complexity and volume for small-size parts, and final products are used in a
broad range of industrial, commercial, medical, dental, firearms, aerospace,
and automotive applications. MIM can produce parts where  it is difficult, or
even impossible, to efficiently manufacture an item through other means of
fabrication. Increased costs for traditional manufacturing methods inherent to
part complexity, such as internal/external threads, miniaturization or identity
marking, typically do not increase the cost in a MIM operation due to the
flexibility of injection molding. Hence, such features would make MIM an ideal
candidate for jewelry manufacturing; however, the high initial costs of the injection
molding tool limit the field to volume applications such as watch cases, cellular
telephone components or sunglasses accessories.9,10 To address the volume-driven
restraints of the MIM process for small-scale applications, sinter-based additive

     Vat-Polymerization (VP)Burkhardt     Vat-polymerization, better known as stereolithography (SLA), is an early and
     widely used additive manufacturing technology for individual pieces. The
    modern layered approach to stereolithography by using ultraviolet light to cure
     photosensitive polymers was first invented in the early 1980s, allowing the creation
      of highly detailed and precise polymer parts.11,12 It works by focusing an ultraviolet
     (UV) laser onto a vat of photopolymer resin.13 With the help of computer-aided
     manufacturing or computer-aided design (CAM/CAD) software, a UV laser or
      digital light processor (DLP) is used to draw or project a pre-programmed design
     or shape onto the surface of the photopolymer vat. Photopolymers are sensitive to
      ultraviolet light, so the resin is photochemically solidified and forms a single layer
      of the desired 3D object. Then, the build platform lowers one layer and a blade
      recoats the top of the tank with resin.12 This process is repeated for each layer of
     the design until the 3D object is complete. Completed parts must be washed with
     a solvent to clean wet resin off their surfaces. Figure 2 illustrates a typical SLA
     system.

   The Lithography-Based metal Manufacturing
   (LMM) Process
   LMM consists of four consecutive steps, as illustrated in Figure 4.





         Figure 4 Processing steps of lithography-based metal manufacturing (schematic)

     After the design of the part in a CAD system (or the generation of the geometrical
     information with help of a 3D scanner as in reverse engineering), the data is
     converted into an STL file and transferred to the printer. In the cooled and
     humidity-controlled printing chamber, the feedstock mixture of metal powder
    and photopolymer is stored in a material reservoir which is equipped with a
     piston that moves in the Z-axis (A) in Figure 5a. The feedstock has a butter-like
     consistency in its cooled state. When heated, the feedstock becomes liquid and
     can be finely distributed with the help of a heated blade (B in Figure 5a). A fine
      layer (typically between 20 and 50 µm) of feedstock provided from reservoir (A)
       is applied to the surface of the working chamber (C in Figure 5a), which is then
     exposed with UV light to such areas where the green part is printed (D in Figure
      5b). The piston of the working chamber is now moving downwards by the height
      of one layer and the process is repeated. Multiple parts can be printed at one time,
     as shown in a close-up of the working chamber surface in Figure 5c.

Thermal debinding of the photopolymer and the sintering of the part to its
final density are done in a two-step operation in a MIM sintering furnace
under protective atmosphere. For the debinding step, the green parts are held

decomposed. A constant flow of protective gas ensures that the decomposed
binder residues are removed from the samples and transported outside the
sintering retort through a piping and exhaust system. In the sintering step, the
parts are quickly heated to a temperature near the melting point of the material
to densify the particles using capillary forces. This results in nearly pore-free
samples with complex shapes and fine-grained microstructure. Figure 7 illustrates

C Burkhardt, N Brito, and M Mungenast. Lithography-based metal manufacturing of jewelry and watch cases made from 316l stainless steel and titanium alloys. Unknown journal, 2022.

The provided excerpt introduces LMM as a sinter-based additive manufacturing technology combining vat-polymerization with principles from metal injection molding, but it does not report the requested measured properties for LMM or metal vat-photopolymerized parts made from 316L stainless steel, 17-4PH stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, or copper. It also contains no tensile values (ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, or elongation) and no surface-roughness measurements for those materials. The only quantitative comparison baseline presented is for conventional MIM: sintering produces approximately 15–25% linear shrinkage and final densification of approximately 96–99% of theoretical solid density. The excerpt states that MIM end products have mechanical and physical properties comparable to annealed conventionally manufactured parts, but it gives no specific UTS, yield strength, elongation, or roughness values. Therefore, the requested material-by-material comparison cannot be established from pages 1–4; additional pages or external studies containing LMM/metal-vat-photopolymerization test data are needed.

## pqac-00000028

From text 'burkhardt2022lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 4-8'.

C Burkhardt, N Brito, and M Mungenast. Lithography-based metal manufacturing of jewelry and watch cases made from 316l stainless steel and titanium alloys. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt does not provide numerical sintering density, linear shrinkage, tensile properties (ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, or elongation), or surface-roughness values for 316L stainless steel, 17-4PH stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, or copper produced by LMM or metal vat photopolymerization. It only gives general process-level information: after debinding and sintering, LMM parts are described as fully dense and nearly pore-free, with a fine-grained microstructure. The printed green parts shrink by approximately 20% overall during sintering, and the shrinkage is reported to be reproducible and similar in all three dimensions; the exact factor depends on material composition. The excerpt also states that LMM uses a two-step debinding and sintering cycle in a MIM furnace, and compares the resulting parts qualitatively with laser powder-bed fusion rather than with MIM properties. Thus, it cannot support a quantitative comparison of density, mechanical properties, or surface roughness against MIM parts. The only MIM-related implication is that LMM applies MIM-style furnace processing and uses predictable isotropic shrinkage, allowing CAD scaling.

Abstract:
Rising demands for miniaturization in industries such as aerospace and electronics have motivated advancements in metal additive manufacturing (AM), resulting in downscaled strategies using direct-energy deposition (DED) processes, now termed micro-DED (µ-DED). Within this context, micro gas metal arc DED (μ-GMA) has demonstrated the ability to deposit layers approximately 1 mm wide with a build rate of 30 cm3/h, positioning this technology between GMA-based DED and other µ-DED processes in terms of regarding dimensional accuracy and build rate. Despite promising initial results, further evaluation of the process impact on the microstructure and mechanical behavior of various alloys is necessary due to the pioneering nature of μ-GMA. The present work focuses on the evaluation of the microstructure (via scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive spectroscopy, thermodynamic simulations, and electron backscatter diffraction analyses) and mechanical behavior (using nanoindentation maps) of single-layer depositions of low alloy and stainless steels using μ-GMA. In addition, traditional GMA-based DED using larger diameter wires was employed to deposit comparably alloys for further discussion. μ-GMA successively deposited a low-alloy steel with a microstructure composed of ferrite and martensite–austenite constituents, achieving a nanohardness (NH) of 3.1 GPa and an elastic modulus (NE) of 196 GPa. In addition, μ-GMA additively manufactured stainless steel with a microstructure composed of a γ matrix and δ-ferrite, exhibiting an NH of 3.7 GPa and an NE of 188 GPa. These results for both deposited materials are comparable to those reported in the literature for regular GMA-based DED depositions, indicating that this new variant has promising potential as a printing technology for small and detailed parts.

Abstract:
Porous metals fabricated via three-dimensional (3D) printing have attracted extensive attention in many fields owing to their open pores and customization potential. However, dense internal structures produced by the powder bed fusion technique fails to meet the feature of porous materials in scenarios that demand large specific surface areas. Herein, we propose a strategy for 3D printing of titanium scaffolds featuring multiscale porous internal structures via powder modification and digital light processing (DLP). After modification, the titanium powders were composited with acrylic resin and maintained spherical shapes. Compared with the raw powder slurries, the modified powder slurries exhibited higher stability and preferable curing characteristics, and the depth sensitivity of the modified powder slurries with 45 vol% solid loading increased by approximately 72%. Green scaffolds were subsequently printed from the slurries with a solid loading reaching 45 vol% via DLP 3D printing. The scaffolds had macropores (pore diameters of approximately 1 mm) and internal open micropores (pore diameters of approximately 5.7–13.0 μm) after sintering. Additionally, these small-featured (approximately 320 μm) scaffolds retained sufficient compressive strength ((70.01 ± 3.53) MPa) even with high porosity (approximately 73.95%). This work can facilitate the fabrication of multiscale porous metal scaffolds with high solid loading slurries, offering potential for applications requiring high specific surface area ratios.

The excerpt provides general information relevant to the sintering challenges of aluminum and other oxidation-sensitive metal powders, but it does not specifically discuss vat photopolymerization or the named Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, titanium, tungsten, molybdenum, or Cu-Cr-Zr systems. Its central point is that native oxide films on metal powders can inhibit metal-atom diffusion, causing poor sintering or requiring higher sintering temperatures. The passage describes replacing a stable native oxide—for example, Al2O3 on aluminum—with a less stable coating such as ZnO, deposited by ALD or ALD-like methods, to promote diffusion and reduce the thermal energy needed for sintering. It also notes that oxidation and water absorption can alter elemental composition and powder rheology. Thin H2O/O2 barrier coatings, hydrophobic surface modifications, and optional vacuum drying are presented as ways to limit oxidation, moisture uptake, and environmental reactions. The excerpt emphasizes that coating selection and atmosphere control matter because oxygen, water, sulfur, nitrogen, and other species can react with powder or parts. However, it contains no explicit discussion of carbon pickup, carbon-containing binders, required inert or reducing atmospheres, exact sintering temperatures, refractory-metal processing limits, alloy-specific phase behavior, or why aluminum might be impossible to process by sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization.

Abstract
Porous metals fabricated via three-dimensional (3D) printing have attracted extensive attention
in many fields owing to their open pores and customization potential. However, dense internal
structures produced by the powder bed fusion technique fails to meet the feature of porous
materials in scenarios that demand large specific surface areas. Herein, we propose a strategy
for 3D printing of titanium scaffolds featuring multiscale porous internal structures via powder
modification and digital light processing (DLP). After modification, the titanium powders were
composited with acrylic resin and maintained spherical shapes. Compared with the raw powder
slurries, the modified powder slurries exhibited higher stability and preferable curing
characteristics, and the depth sensitivity of the modified powder slurries with 45 vol% solid
loading increased by approximately 72%. Green scaffolds were subsequently printed from the
slurries with a solid loading reaching 45 vol% via DLP 3D printing. The scaffolds had
macropores (pore diameters of approximately 1 mm) and internal open micropores (pore
diameters of approximately 5.7–13.0 µm) after sintering. Additionally, these small-featured
(approximately 320 µm) scaffolds retained sufficient compressive strength

       Figures 3.6a and 3.6b show the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of BJT and µDLP

microstructures, taken using  electron  backscatter  diffraction (EBSD) imaging. As

observed in the previous micrographs, both the BJT and µDLP microstructures showed a

homogenous distribution of equiaxed grains with the inclusion of annealing twins. A weak


                                47texture was recorded for both microstructures, as expected after sintering. Most of the

remaining porosity within the microstructures after sintering was located intragranularly.

This indicated that porosity elimination in the final stage of sintering could no longer have

occurred by grain boundary diffusion and instead required diffusion through the lattice

[20]. The average grain size was recorded as 31.5 ±12.4 µm and 43.3 ±16.1 µm for BJT

and µDLP, respectively. The significant standard deviation indicated a large grain size

distribution throughout the microstructure but was primarily due to the inclusion of small-

sized annealing twin boundaries. Although the starting PSD was lower for µDLP than

BJT, their average grain size was similar in magnitude, implying that more grain growth

occurred during the sintering treatment of the µDLP sample. The low volume fraction of

δ-ferrite within the µDLP sample may also reinforce the hypothesis that a higher sintering

temperature or longer sintering time was utilized, allowing for greater diffusion of ferrite

into the austenite matrix. Alternatively, a combination of either δ-ferrite and/or porosity

may have impeded grain growth in the BJT sample by a Zener pinning mechanism [51].

       Figures 3.6c and 3.6d show the IPF maps of SLM and µSLM microstructures in

the <110> direction //BD consisting of melt pools and a mixture of equiaxed and epitaxial

grains. A weak texture for the PBF samples was observed. The anisotropic properties

exhibited in PBF materials have been reported to exist not only due to the epitaxial grain

growth but are more dependent on the local texture, which is typically oriented in the

<101> //BD corresponding to a green color in the IPF map [49,52]. The lack of a strong

texture was due to incorporating a 67° rotation angle between powder layers. Rotating the

laser scan path allowed for a more even distribution of layer-penetrating, volumetric

thermal gradients across the new surface, introducing a cycle of remelting and partial

measurement of PBF components using EBSD analysis, an area averaging scheme was

utilized with the OIM software, consisting of a summation of Area/Area Fraction of pixels

within grains to find a result in units of µm2 and then taking its square root. This method

does not require a spherical grain shape to measure grain size accurately and was chosen

due to the heterogeneous grain morphology in SLM components. The average grain size

was recorded as 24.5 ±12.9 µm and 19.2 ±9.5 µm for the SLM and µSLM samples,

                                493.4.3 Mechanical Properties


       Table 5 summarizes measured mechanical properties, including room temperature

uniaxial tensile properties, microhardness, grain size, density, and surface roughness for

each printing process and sample condition. The AM tensile bars were tested in their as

printed and machined conditions to address a change in surface quality. The micro-AM

tensile bars were tested at two thicknesses of 100 µm and 250 µm to record properties at

scale for applications with specific dimensional requirements. Figure 3.7 shows the

resultant tensile curves, plotted as engineering stress and strain. Due to the innate source

of error accompanied with mounting foil-like micro-AM tensile bars in a custom sample

fixture, premature failure was recorded throughout the elastic region for a few tensile

curves. A magnitude of 190 GPa is reported as Young’s Modulus of 316L stainless steel,

but the largest experimental result recorded was 139 GPa with poor repeatability. Due to

the inconsistency of measured modulus values, Young’s Modulus was omitted from the

report. A large standard deviation was recorded for a few tensile measurements due to

inconsistent results or low success rates during testing. For this reason, the recorded tensile

properties of the micro-AM conditions should be taken as an approximation. An

approximate strain rate of 0.001 s-1 was maintained across all AM and micro-AM testing

conditions.

      The BJT and µDLP samples performed relatively identically, with an average YS

of ~190 MPa, a UTS of ~540 MPa, and an elongation at fracture between 50-75%. Table

5 also  lists comparable microhardness, grain  size,  density, and measured surface

roughness  for  each  tensile  condition. The  similarity  in  tensile  properties  and

microhardness between BJT and µDLP could be attributed to their similar grain size. The

                                563.5 Conclusions


   This study investigated 316L stainless steel components produced by sinter-based

additive manufacturing and powder bed fusion technologies, examining both additive and

micro-additive techniques. Based on the combination of microstructural characterization

and mechanical testing, the following conclusions were made:

1  The SBAM samples were printed with ≥ 96% bulk density, while the PBF samples

   were printed with ≥ ~98% bulk density. The micro-AM samples recorded bulk

    densities ≥ 99% using estimated area fraction measurements but could not be

    accurately verified with an Archimedes method measurement due to their low weight

   and small size.

2  No significant qualitative difference in microstructure was observed between the AM

   and micro-AM processes. The only difference between both SBAM samples was their

    δ-ferrite volume fractions due to their respective sintering conditions. The PBF

   samples mainly differed in average grain and cell size, consisting of similar melt pool

    structures and chemical micro-segregation. Measured alloy compositions for  all

   samples were similar to the reference standard, suggesting that both AM, and micro-

  AM processes did not adversely change the alloy system.

3  There was no significant quantitative difference in mechanical performance between

    the BJT and µDLP samples. The SBAM samples exhibited a trend of lower UTS, with

    values of ~550 MPa, and higher elongation, up to 76%, compared to PBF samples. An

   average grain size of 31.5 µm and 43.3 µm for BJT and µDLP, respectively, justified

    the similarity in mechanical properties by the Hall-Petch mechanism. The 1-3%

    difference in bulk density resulted in higher mechanical properties for the µDLP


                                57   samples. Overall, the measured properties for the SBAM samples met the minimum

    required mechanical performance set by ASTM B883  / MPIF 35 standards and

    industry results provided by Desktop Metal.

4  The SLM and SLM samples exhibited a trend of higher strength, up to ~750 MPa,

4.2 Introduction


      Metal additive manufacturing (MAM) refers to a collection of technologies that

utilize metal feedstock (wire, powder, or sheets) to build up three-dimensional solid metal

components in a layer-by-layer process. Unlike traditional manufacturing processes,

MAM offers the advantages of fabricating near-net-shaped parts with complex geometries

and greater design freedom utilizing computer-aided design models [1-2]. The first known

technology, selective laser sintering, was invented in 1989 and introduced the capability

to fuse feedstock material by heating near or above  its melting temperature. Metal

feedstock can either be fused during a single-step printing process with the use of a high-

energy input (e.g., laser or electron beam) or with a two-step “print and sinter” process

involving the fabrication of a green part before a sintering heat treatment [1, 3]. The latter

two-step process encompasses a category of technologies under the umbrella term of

sinter-based additive manufacturing (SBAM), the most popular of which is metal binder

jetting (BJT).

      Metal binder jetting is a process that utilizes a powder bed substrate and selective

infiltration of binder material from inkjet nozzles to adhere powder feedstock together,

layer-by-layer [4]. A debinding step is then utilized to remove any binder from the printed

three-dimensional component,  known as a green part (consolidated powder particles

                                60before sintering). The green part is then sintered to allow the consolidated powder particles

to fuse, densifying and shrinking the component into its final shape [5]. The benefit of

temporarily adhering powder together, rather than fusing them, during the first stage of

printing is the lack of thermal processing. This drastically increases the available library

of printable materials, as it would only be restricted based on sintering temperature rather

than melting temperature. Additionally, the rise in popularity for most SBAM processes

is due to their combination of fabricating components with better surface resolution, a

lower cost per part, and a higher production speed per part compared to fusion-based

MAM [6-7].

       This rise in popularity for SBAM complements the demand for micro-sized

components in industrial applications. Since its conception in 2003, the number of micro-

metal additive manufacturing (MMAM) technologies has continued to increase, as it has

been identified as an effective fabrication method for low to medium-volume production

of highly complex, high-resolution components [8-10]. Material jetting is an AM process

generally suitable for polymeric materials.  Still, recent technology incorporates the

SBAM approach, allowing for the fabrication of small-sized components using metallic

or ceramic materials. Nano-Particle Jetting™ (NPJ), developed by X-JET,  utilizes

powderless, nano-sized particles suspended within a liquid formula to be deposited onto

a substrate as droplets from inkjet nozzles [11]. The print head, consisting of thousands of

inkjet nozzles, selectively jets a thin layer (as low as 8 µm) of liquid droplets and support

material onto the substrate. Each liquid droplet (single  pico-liters) contains metal

nanoparticles of varying morphology, which, when subsequently dried, evaporate so that

only the nanoparticles remain. This process is estimated to be about five times faster in



                                61production speed than powder bed fusion. After printing, the support material is dissolved

through the debinding step before the final sintering heat treatment, similar to metal binder

jetting [12]. With a much lower layer thickness than other MAM processes, a better

surface finish and dimensional accuracy can be achieved without compromising the

overall production time. In addition, the process avoids potentially harmful working

environments through exposure to powder or resin. Currently, 316L stainless steel is the

only commercially available metal alloy for nano-particle jetting. Although capable of

producing metal components, most reported literature on nano-particle jetting focuses on

producing ceramic components or incorporating metal nano-particle infiltration during a

BJT  process  [12-13]. As  a  result,  a  limited  understanding  is  available  for  the

microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of metal alloys produced by NPJ,

both in their as-sintered condition and after post-processing. A major disadvantage of

components produced by SBAM is relatively low final density, so post-processing is

necessary for specific applications.

      Hot  isostatic  pressing (HIP) was invented  in 1955  for  diffusion bonding

applications, but within the MAM industry, it is primarily used as a post-process heat

treatment. The main objective of HIP is to eliminate porosity or other microstructural

defects within a bulk material, which may exist after fabrication. The HIP process utilizes

heated gas  (e.g., argon, nitrogen, or helium) under isostatic pressure, with current

equipment utilizing temperatures up to 2200 °C and gas pressures between several 10’s to

~200 MPa [14-15]. A critical flow stress is required to begin the densification process,

which can be achieved with varied combinations of temperature and pressure. In the case

of 316L stainless steel, the ideal temperature generally ranges between 1100-1160 °C, but



                                62inconsistencies exist in literature as to the ideal pressure for this range. HIP parameters

for most MAM processes are currently based on ASTM standards for either powder bed

fusion or metal injection molding, which require a minimum pressure of 100-103 MPa

[16-17]. Studies reported by Kumar and Cooper utilized these minimum pressures and

reported an improvement in density after HIP [18-19]. Alternatively, a pressure of 130-

140 MPa is more commonly reported in literature, utilized by Mao, Zhang, and Grech as

the default pressure used in industry [20-22]. Furthermore, the benefits of pressures >140

MPa  are highly  debated. Liverani and Grech  reported  either  insignificant  or no

improvement to densification utilizing pressures of ~200 MPa, whereas Cegan and

Puichaud reported pressures of 190 MPa and 180 MPa, respectively, were necessary to

reduce nano-sized porosity within the microstructure [23-25]. With all this in mind, most

of the reported literature involving HIP of 316L stainless steel MAM has been published

for systems related to powder bed fusion and has yet to extensively investigate its effects

for metal binder jetting and metal material jetting.

      The final variable of a well-controlled HIP cycle is time. Soak times at the target

temperature/pressure range between 1-4 hours, but full cycles can last over 10 hours with

the required steps to raise and lower temperature and pressure. This may be of concern as

the extended time at elevated temperatures can cause microstructural coarsening or the

formation of secondary phases. The long cycle times due to slow cooling or the use of

high temperatures and pressures can also be expensive, which is a major impediment to

the implementation of HIP [15]. In an effort to minimize the long cycling time, modern

HIP equipment has incorporated uniform rapid cooling (URC) (with a cooling rate of ~200

°C/min), allowing for densification and a controlled heat treatment to be performed within



                                63a single process [26-27]. Although the overall goal of HIP is to produce fully dense

components, the access to modern equipment with a concurrent heat treatment allows the

freedom  to  tailor  final microstructures and mechanical  properties required of the

application. Ultimately, the purpose of this research is to characterize metal material jetted

(nano-particle jetting) 316L stainless steel components as they compare to metal binder

jetting. The study was separated into two parts: (1) a brief comparison between HIP with

standard cooling and HIP with uniform rapid cooling and (2) a characterization of the

resultant microstructure and mechanical performance of each SBAM process in their as-

sintered and HIP’ed conditions.

Abstract:
Ceramic nanocomposites, containing at least one phase in the nanometric dimension, have received special interest in recent years. They have, in fact, demonstrated increased performance, reliability and lifetime with respect to monolithic ceramics. However, a successful approach to the production of tailored composite nanostructures requires the development of innovative concepts at each step of manufacturing, from the synthesis of composite nanopowders, to their processing and sintering. This review aims to deepen understanding of some of the critical issues associated with the manufacturing of nanocomposite ceramics, focusing on alumina-based composite systems. Two case studies are presented and briefly discussed. The former illustrates the benefits, in terms of sintered microstructure and related mechanical properties, resulting from the application of an engineering approach to a laboratory-scale protocol for the elaboration of nanocomposites in the system alumina-ZrO2-YAG (yttrium aluminium garnet). The latter illustrates the manufacturing of alumina-based composites for large-scale applications such as cutting tools, carried out by an injection molding process. The need for an engineering approach to be applied in all processing steps is demonstrated also in this second case study, where a tailored manufacturing process is required to obtain the desired results.

- 316L µDLP (Pires 2025): YS 187-194, UTS 533-579, El 50-76%, density 96-99%, Ra 1.7-2.7, grain 43µm
- 316L BJT (Pires 2025): YS 185-191, UTS 532-542, El 66-72%, density 96-98%, Ra 2.7, grain 31.5µm
- 316L ASTM B883/MPIF 35: YS 140-175, UTS 450-520, El 40-50%, density 96%
- Ti-6Al-4V LMM (Harakaly/Incus 2025): YS ~900, UTS ~960, C=0.11wt% (spec max 0.08%)
- Incus general: Ra <2µm, tolerances ±0.5%, min wall 0.1mm
- Greene Group/Holo: min wall 0.07mm, max wall 3.5mm, tolerance ±0.025mm up to 12mm, Ra 0.8-1.6µm

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Supported by literature | Contradicted or materially qualified by literature | No independent data located |
|---|---|---|
| **Incus LMM can achieve as-sintered Ra below 2 µm.** Incus-affiliated reports state Ra below 2 µm, while independent µDLP 316L measurements of Ra = 1.71–2.69 µm support the general magnitude, though not every alloy and orientation (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000038) | **“Ti-6Al-4V meets medical-grade chemistry.”** Incus reported about **0.11 wt.% C**, exceeding the cited **0.08 wt.%** limit, despite strengths of approximately 900 MPa YS and 960 MPa UTS (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000031) | **Holo/Greene pure copper above 92% IACS.** No independently measured conductivity dataset for PureForm copper was located; oxide, carbon residue, porosity, and atmosphere strongly affect conductivity (pqac-00000008) |
| **µDLP 316L meets the quoted ASTM B883/MPIF Standard 35 MIM tensile minima.** Measured YS was 186.5–193.7 MPa, UTS 533.7–579.4 MPa, and elongation 50.9–76.1%, versus quoted ranges of 140–175 MPa, 450–520 MPa, and 40–50% (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039) | **“Any metal is processable.”** GRCop-42’s Cr₂Nb phase makes pressureless solid-state sintering impractical; Cr and Nb also oxidized under trace moisture. Aluminum metal was not demonstrated in the retrieved metal-VPP evidence, and its stable Al₂O₃ film is a diffusion barrier (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000041) | **Greene Group’s 0.07 mm minimum wall in 17-4PH and 316L.** The closest published Incus result found was a general minimum wall of at least 0.10 mm, not an independent test of Greene’s process (pqac-00000026) |
| **Approximately 20% linear shrinkage is credible.** Incus-related work reports about 20% shrinkage, reproducible and similar in all three dimensions; conventional MIM commonly spans approximately 15–25% (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | **Blanket “MIM-equivalent” claim.** Selected 316L tensile results are MIM-like, but the exposure-defined crosslinked binder has different solvent-accessibility, decomposition, gas-transport, and cracking risks. A generic MIM cycle is not evidence of equivalence for every formulation, geometry, or alloy (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015) | **Greene Group’s 3.5 mm maximum wall.** No independent geometry-specific debinding study validating this limit was located; thick and closed sections are recognized debinding risks (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000016) |
| **Fine MIM-grade powder is compatible with LMM.** Incus reports routinely using gas-atomized MIM-grade powder with a **0–25 µm size distribution**. This supports sub-25-µm feedstock, but does not establish D50 below 25 µm as a universal requirement (pqac-00000019) | **Universal “fully dense” claim.** Reported sinter-based densities vary with process and method: approximately 92–98% is reported without vacuum or sintering aids, while miniature µDLP 316L sections gave image-based estimates near 99.2–99.3% (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039) | **Greene Group’s ±0.025 mm tolerance through 12 mm.** Published Incus-related evidence instead gives a broader typical tolerance of ±0.5%; no independent study reproduced Greene’s tighter absolute tolerance (pqac-00000026) |
| **Many geometries can be printed without sacrificial printed supports.** Incus demonstrated densely nested jewelry and watch-case geometries using surrounding feedstock as green support. Furnace setters and cleaning access may still be required (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000007) | **Unqualified “support-free” interpretation.** Surrounding paste may support printing, but it must be removed from channels, and weak brown or sintering parts can sag or require setters. “No printed supports” does not eliminate complete-process support constraints (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) | **Incus maximum wall of about 10 mm.** No independent, section-thickness-resolved debinding validation was located. Published work cautions that thick or closed regions may debind slowly (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| **Layer thicknesses of 20–50 µm are demonstrated for Incus LMM.** Heated-blade film coating and UV exposure were reported over this range (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030) | **Projector pixel size equals final resolution or tolerance.** Scattering, overcure, cleaning, shrinkage, registration, and sintering alter final dimensions; pixel pitch alone is not a defensible final-part resolution metric (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000009) | **17-4PH-specific tensile and fatigue properties.** Commercial availability was reported, but no independent 17-4PH tensile or fatigue dataset for this route was located (pqac-00000026) |
| **MIM-like 316L microstructure and properties are possible.** µDLP 316L showed equiaxed grains with annealing twins, approximately 43.3 µm mean grain size, high ductility, and performance similar to a matched binder-jetted comparator (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) | **Ti-6Al-4V is already fully qualified for implants.** Incus explicitly described further development as necessary to reach medical-grade composition; strength alone does not establish implant qualification (pqac-00000020) | **Fatigue data for structural metals made by this route.** No independent S–N, strain-life, crack-growth, or orientation-resolved fatigue dataset was located; density and monotonic tensile strength cannot substitute for fatigue testing (pqac-00000008) |
| **Fine metal features are feasible but system-specific.** A 35 µm feature was reported in one 316L system, while Incus demonstrated 150 µm-wide and 50 µm-deep surface dimples; neither establishes a universal limit (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020) | **One shrinkage factor is universally transferable.** Even where near-isotropic bulk shrinkage is reported, local packing, geometry, gravity, setter friction, furnace position, and chemistry can produce anisotropic or geometry-dependent distortion (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | **Corrosion performance for 17-4PH, 316L, Ti-6Al-4V, or copper.** No independent polarization, pitting, salt-spray, immersion, or stress-corrosion dataset specific to this route was located (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000020) |
